hints: Look at the shape of the melting point trend, a very high value followed by three very low values tells you a lot about structure and bonding.
Notice that element A has a giant melting point while B, C and D are all near or below 273 K, so A must be a giant covalent solid and the others are simple molecular.
Recall how melting point changes across Period 3 from Si to Cl, with a peak at silicon then low values for P, S and Cl, and link that to Group 14 to 17.
walkthrough:
**Spot the giant structure**

Think like a detective. One element, A, has a hugely higher melting point than the other three.

That is the classic sign of a giant covalent lattice with many strong covalent bonds to break, while B, C and D with melting points around 273 K or below must be simple molecules with only weak van der Waals forces.

**Find which period fits**

All proton numbers are less than 20, so we are in Period 2 or Period 3.

In Period 3, the pattern is: $\text{Si}$ (giant, mp ~1683 K), then $\text{P}$, $\text{S}$, $\text{Cl}$ (all simple molecular, mp < 400 K). This matches the graph shape perfectly: very high, then low, slightly up, then down.

**Assign Groups 14 to 17**

If A is Group 14 ($\text{Si}$), then the consecutive elements must be:
$$\text{A (Group 14) } \rightarrow \text{ B (Group 15) } \rightarrow \text{ C (Group 16) } \rightarrow \text{ D (Group 17)}$$

**Identify Group 16**

Group 16 in Period 3 is sulfur, $\text{S}$. It has a slightly higher melting point than phosphorus because $\text{S}_8$ is larger than $\text{P}_4$ and has stronger van der Waals forces.

That small rise from B to C followed by a fall to D confirms C is the Group 16 element.

options.A: A has the very high melting point, so it is the giant covalent element. In Period 3 this is Si in Group 14, not Group 16.
options.B: B is the first low melting point after the giant structure, so it is the Group 15 element (P). Students sometimes pick the lowest point, but Group 15 is slightly lower than Group 16 due to smaller molecules.
options.C: C is correct. After Si (A) and P (B), C shows the small increase in melting point expected for S in Group 16, because S8 has stronger van der Waals forces than P4, before falling again to Cl.
options.D: D has the lowest melting point below 273 K, which fits Cl2 in Group 17. It has the smallest molecules and weakest van der Waals forces, so it melts lowest, not Group 16.
